(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) — Beware: another bloated, overproduced, high-concept creation has emerged from the DreamWorks Animation laboratory, seemingly ready to devour your children. In *Monsters vs. Aliens*, Susan—also known as “Ginormica”—must save the world.

Still, there is little real cause for alarm. *Monsters vs. Aliens* is ultimately relatively harmless: a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a rather flimsy excuse for a plot.

That may sound harsh. After all, who would not want to watch a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles—the ultimate demolition roller derby? But consider that image for just a moment. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Attempt the same feat with motorcars and you would not get very far.

Is that too picky? Perhaps. Yet Pixar would hardly treat the laws of physics so casually, and that kind of inattention to detail is characteristic of the lackadaisical storytelling on display here, as well as in other DreamWorks animated features. Incidentally, the talent pool for this film includes the directors of *Shrek 2* and *Shark Tale*, and the writers of *Kung Fu Panda* and *The Rocker*.

High concepts, first-rate voice talent, and scattershot pop-cultural references are no substitute for a coherent script. The XXXL woman in question—dubbed “Ginormica” by her U.S. military guards—begins as plain, petite Susan Murphy, voiced by Reese Witherspoon. Minutes before she is due to marry the unctuous chauvinist Derek, voiced by Paul Rudd, she is struck by a meteorite. Her sudden growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if, at first glance, her new roommates do not appear to offer much of an improvement.

They include Dr. Cockroach, voiced by Hugh Laurie, a mad scientist who semi-inadvertently mutates with a bug; B.O.B., voiced by Seth Rogen, an amorphous blue, jelly-like blob who gets along perfectly well without a brain; Missing Link, voiced by Will Arnett, a gung-ho amphibian who is all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus, who is not voiced by anyone because he has nothing to say.

Science-fiction fans may enjoy tallying the references to a host of classics—*Close Encounters of the Third Kind*, *Invaders from Mars*, *The Fly*, *The Creature from the Black Lagoon*, *The Blob*, *Mothra*, and *Attack of the 50-Foot Woman*, for starters—and noting a few clever touches, such as Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffing on George C. Scott in *Dr. Strangelove*.

The problem is that, once the introductions are complete, the filmmakers have little to offer beyond a desperately limp plot: the White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from the evil Gallaxhar, voiced by Rainn Wilson, a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, who employs a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work.

Ginormica receives a kick-butt finale and is, in numerous respects, a far stronger character than the movie’s president—who, in a genuinely witty casting touch, is voiced by Stephen Colbert. That may be good politics, or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio’s perspective. It has been some time since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character, unless one counts *Coraline*, which was far too frightening for my family. Even so, Susan’s self-esteem is an awfully long time coming.

iReport.com: What do you think of *Monsters vs. Aliens*?

Bizarrely—and perhaps it is only my imagination—Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. One wonders: would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?

Visually, too, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be less apparent if one seeks out the 3-D version. It is curious how often 3-D films produce two-dimensional characters, with *Coraline* once again proving the exception to the rule.

Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, *Monsters vs. Aliens* ought to be a great deal of fun—and, at times, it is. But the truth is that it is as absorbed in itself as Susan’s preening fiancé. Hand on heart, I had a better time at *Space Chimps*.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For *Entertainment Weekly*’s take, click here.

(CNN) — Beware: DreamWorks Animation has released another oversized, slickly manufactured, idea-driven spectacle, and this one is aimed straight at children. In *Monsters vs. Aliens*, Susan — later renamed “Ginormica” — is tasked with rescuing the planet.

Still, there is no need to panic too much. The movie is fairly innocuous: a mild, toothless spoof with an automatic feminist angle and a very thin storyline. That may sound severe. After all, who wouldn’t be amused by the sight of a 50-foot woman tearing through San Francisco on “skates” that are actually cars — essentially a giant destructive roller derby?

But pause on that image for a moment. Roller skates function because their wheels are fixed in place. Substitute automobiles, and the concept falls apart quickly. Is that an overly fussy objection? Maybe. But Pixar would be unlikely to treat physics so casually, and that sort of loose attention to detail reflects the careless storytelling found here and in other DreamWorks animated films. For the record, this film’s creative team includes the directors of *Shrek 2* and *Shark Tale*, along with writers from *Kung Fu Panda* and *The Rocker*.

Big premises, famous voice actors and a barrage of pop-culture nods cannot replace a script that actually holds together.

The enormous heroine — nicknamed “Ginormica” by the U.S. military personnel guarding her — begins as ordinary, small-framed Susan Murphy, voiced by Reese Witherspoon. Moments before she is due to marry the slick, sexist Derek, played by Paul Rudd, she is struck by a meteorite. The impact causes her to grow dramatically, sparing her from that grim marital future, though her new companions do not immediately seem like a major upgrade.

Among them are Dr. Cockroach, voiced by Hugh Laurie, a deranged scientist who accidentally — or nearly accidentally — fused himself with an insect; B.O.B., voiced by Seth Rogen, a shapeless blue gelatinous mass who manages perfectly well despite having no brain; Missing Link, voiced by Will Arnett, an aggressive amphibian with plenty of attitude; and Insectosaurus, a gigantic dust mite who has no voice actor because he has nothing to say.

Science-fiction devotees may enjoy spotting the many allusions to classics such as *Close Encounters of the Third Kind*, *Invaders from Mars*, *The Fly*, *The Creature from the Black Lagoon*, *The Blob*, *Mothra* and *Attack of the 50-Foot Woman*, among others. There are also a few genuinely clever touches, including Kiefer Sutherland’s General W.R. Monger, who echoes George C. Scott in *Dr. Strangelove*.

The problem is that after the characters have been introduced, the movie has little more to offer than a weak plot. The White House recruits these monster-like heroes to defend Earth from the villainous Gallaxhar, voiced by Rainn Wilson — a squid-shaped alien with four eyes and eight legs — along with a one-eyed metal robot that carries out his orders.

Ginormica is given a forceful finale, and she emerges as a far more powerful figure, in several senses, than the film’s president. In one of the movie’s smarter casting choices, the president is voiced by Stephen Colbert. From a studio standpoint, this may be smart politics, or at least smart marketing: it has been some time since a family animated film offered a truly strong female lead, unless one counts *Coraline*, which was much too frightening for my household. Even so, Susan takes an awfully long time to arrive at real confidence.

iReport.com asks: What do you think of *Monsters vs. Aliens*?

Oddly — unless I am imagining it — Gallaxhar looks a little like President Obama. If so, does that make Susan/Ginormica some kind of stand-in for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?

The film is not especially impressive visually either, though its weaknesses may be less obvious in the 3-D version. It is curious how often 3-D films end up giving audiences flat characters — with *Coraline*, once again, being the exception.

Lighthearted, silly and proudly lowbrow, *Monsters vs. Aliens* ought to be a great deal of fun, and occasionally it is. But ultimately, it is almost as self-absorbed as Susan’s vain fiancé. Honestly, I enjoyed *Space Chimps* more.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is 94 minutes long and rated PG. For *Entertainment Weekly*’s review, click here.

DreamWorks Animation’s *Monsters vs. Aliens* is a noisy, overproduced, high-concept animated satire that tries to combine retro monster-movie parody, superhero spectacle, pop-culture comedy, and a lightly feminist story of self-discovery. The film centers on Susan Murphy, a young woman whose wedding day is interrupted when she is struck by a meteor and grows to enormous size. Renamed Ginormica by the government, she is taken to a secret facility where other monsters have been hidden away: the gelatinous B.O.B., the insect-headed Dr. Cockroach, the half-ape half-fish Missing Link, and the gigantic Insectosaurus. When an alien villain threatens Earth, these imprisoned oddities are released and turned into reluctant heroes.

The premise has plenty of potential, especially in the way Susan’s transformation forces her to rethink her identity, her relationship, and the small life she had been expected to accept. There is a recognizable feminist angle in her journey from dutiful fiancée to independent heroine, and the movie occasionally suggests a sharper satire about celebrity culture, government paranoia, and old-fashioned gender roles. However, the film rarely develops those ideas with much care. Instead, it often settles for broad gags, frantic action, and easy references.

The production is bright, loud, and polished, with a cast of celebrity voices working hard to keep the energy up. There are scattered laughs, some clever visual jokes, and enough movement to hold the attention of younger viewers. But the movie’s constant busyness cannot hide the weakness of its storytelling. The plot feels patched together, the supporting monsters are more like comic gimmicks than fully realized characters, and the satire is too unfocused to leave much impact. Pop-culture jokes and large-scale set pieces arrive one after another, but they do not add up to a coherent or emotionally satisfying adventure.

In the end, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is harmless entertainment, but it is also a disappointment. It has the look and sound of a major animated event, and it contains the ingredients for a smart, funny, and empowering film. Yet its reliance on spectacle, celebrity voices, and surface-level parody makes it feel thin. The film may amuse in the moment, but it never becomes as inventive, sharp, or memorable as its concept promises.

counterfactuals.output:
**Review: “Monsters vs. Aliens” is big, bright and busy — but not quite monstrous enough**

DreamWorks Animation’s **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** arrives with a giant heroine, a squad of oddball creatures, a tentacled alien menace and enough pop-culture winks to keep parents awake between bursts of kid-friendly mayhem. It is a slick, frequently funny animated spectacle — especially in 3-D — but beneath its impressive scale and energetic voice work, the film sometimes feels more like a clever package of references than a fully satisfying story.

The plot is pure retro sci-fi pastiche. On her wedding day, Susan Murphy is struck by a meteorite and transformed into a 49-foot-11-inch giant. Renamed **Ginormica** by the government, she is whisked away to a secret facility housing other “monsters”: the brainy insect-human hybrid Dr. Cockroach, the gelatinous B.O.B., the half-ape/half-fish Missing Link and the skyscraper-sized Insectosaurus. When an alien overlord named Gallaxhar threatens Earth, the monsters are recruited as humanity’s last hope.

As storytelling, it’s functional and familiar. The film moves briskly from origin story to prison comedy to alien-invasion action picture, rarely slowing long enough to give its emotional beats much weight. Susan’s journey — from dutiful bride-to-be to self-possessed hero — is the spine of the movie, and it is easily the most engaging part. But the broader narrative leans heavily on set pieces and one-liners, with a villain who is more a comic device than a memorable threat.

Visually, though, **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** shows DreamWorks in confident crowd-pleasing mode. The character designs are deliberately broad and toyetic, but the animation has snap and polish. The action sequences, particularly the Golden Gate Bridge battle, are staged with a strong sense of scale and motion. The film’s 1950s creature-feature influence gives it a fun visual identity, even when the jokes drift into easy territory.

The voice cast does a lot of heavy lifting. **Reese Witherspoon** brings warmth and clarity to Susan/Ginormica, making her more than just a sight gag in a white jumpsuit. **Seth Rogen** gets many of the film’s biggest laughs as B.O.B., a brainless blue blob whose cheerful stupidity is played with expert timing. **Hugh Laurie** is amusingly theatrical as Dr. Cockroach, while **Will Arnett** gives Missing Link a swaggering, washed-up macho energy. **Rainn Wilson’s** Gallaxhar is manic but less distinctive, and **Stephen Colbert’s** blustering President is a broad gag that lands best in small doses.

The film’s feminist themes are surprisingly central, if not always subtle. Susan begins the movie defined by her engagement and by the expectations of a self-absorbed fiancé who wants her to shrink — figuratively, at least — to fit his ambitions. Her transformation into Ginormica becomes a metaphor for taking up space, recognizing her own strength and rejecting a life built around pleasing someone else. For a mainstream animated comedy, that arc is refreshing. Still, the film’s empowerment message is delivered in fairly blunt strokes, and Susan’s internal life could have used more nuance.

As for the pop-culture references, **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** is packed with them: nods to “The Fly,” “The Blob,” “Creature from the Black Lagoon,” “Godzilla,” Cold War paranoia, disaster movies and alien-invasion classics. Some references are witty; others feel like DreamWorks’ familiar strategy of keeping adults entertained through recognition rather than deeper comedy. The result is a movie that often feels fast and funny in the moment, but not especially lasting.

The 3-D presentation is one of the film’s strongest selling points. Rather than feeling like an afterthought, it is built into the movie’s visual design: meteors streak toward the audience, massive robots loom over city streets and action scenes emphasize depth without becoming visually chaotic. It may not transform the film into a classic, but it gives the theatrical experience a genuine sense of event.

In the end, **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** is enjoyable, colorful and technically impressive, with a better heroine than its noisy advertising might suggest. But it also reflects some of DreamWorks Animation’s recurring weaknesses: a reliance on pop-culture riffs, broad caricature and rapid-fire gags over emotional depth. It’s a fun ride — just not quite the towering achievement its heroine becomes.

**Grade: B-**

**Review: “Monsters vs. Aliens” proves bigger is not necessarily better**

DreamWorks Animation’s *Monsters vs. Aliens* arrives with a title that sounds like a punchline and a plot that often feels like one stretched to feature length. It is loud, shiny, and relentlessly busy — the sort of movie that seems convinced that if enough objects fly toward the screen, no one will notice the jokes landing with the grace of a refrigerator dropped from orbit.

Reese Witherspoon voices Susan Murphy, a bride-to-be who, after being struck by a meteor, grows into the towering Ginormica. It’s a promising setup: a woman literally outgrows the small life prescribed for her. Unfortunately, the movie treats that idea with all the subtlety of a neon billboard reading “EMPOWERMENT, NOW IN 3-D.” Witherspoon brings warmth and poise to Ginormica, but she’s trapped in a script that mistakes volume for wit and motion for momentum.

The supporting monsters fare no better. Seth Rogen’s B.O.B., a gelatinous blue blob with one eye and no brain, is meant to provide anarchic comic relief, but his routine wears thin quickly — he’s less a character than a screensaver with a laugh track. Hugh Laurie lends his voice to Dr. Cockroach, a mad scientist with insect parts and almost enough charm to suggest there was once a sharper movie hiding in the laboratory. Almost.

Stephen Colbert, as the President of the United States, has one of the film’s better gags, largely because Colbert’s mock-patriotic absurdity needs little help to function. But even he is thrown into a blender of pop-culture references and kid-friendly chaos that seems engineered more by marketing executives than storytellers.

The problem isn’t that *Monsters vs. Aliens* is silly. Pixar has built masterpieces out of toys, fish, rats, and robots. The problem is that Pixar’s best films remember to put a heart inside the machine. DreamWorks, here, seems more interested in revving the engine and honking the horn. Compared with Pixar’s emotional architecture, this movie feels like a bounce house: colorful, noisy, briefly diverting, and impossible to remember five minutes after leaving.

And then there’s *Coraline*, released the same year — a film that trusted children with strangeness, danger, and visual imagination. Next to that eerie stop-motion jewel, *Monsters vs. Aliens* looks less like a work of animation than a product demonstration for rendering software and Happy Meal tie-ins.

There are flashes of invention, and younger viewers may enjoy the spectacle. But for anyone hoping for the wit of *Shrek*, the emotional precision of Pixar, or the haunting originality of *Coraline*, this monster mash is mostly mush. Ginormica may be 50 feet tall, but the movie around her is disappointingly small.

**“Monsters vs. Aliens”: Big, Bright, and Not Quite Out of This World**

DreamWorks Animation’s **“Monsters vs. Aliens”** arrives with a title that sounds less like a movie than a studio pitch scrawled on a whiteboard: take classic creature-feature misfits, add an invading extraterrestrial menace, stir in celebrity voices, and release in gleaming 3-D. The result is a busy, amiable, intermittently funny animated spectacle that has the look of a major event and the soul of a committee meeting.

The film begins with Susan Murphy, voiced with warm comic earnestness by **Reese Witherspoon**, preparing for her wedding to self-absorbed local TV weatherman Derek Dietl, played by **Paul Rudd**. But just before the ceremony, Susan is struck by a meteorite containing a mysterious substance called quantonium. Instead of merely ruining her dress, the encounter causes her to grow to nearly 50 feet tall. Government agents promptly whisk her away to a secret facility, where she is renamed **Ginormica** and introduced to a group of imprisoned monsters deemed too strange for normal society.

Her fellow detainees are the film’s best comic invention, even when the script doesn’t always know what to do with them. **Seth Rogen** supplies the voice of **B.O.B.**, a cheerful, brainless blue blob with one eye and no digestive system. **Hugh Laurie** voices **Dr. Cockroach, Ph.D.**, a mad scientist who accidentally transformed himself into a human-cockroach hybrid. **Will Arnett** plays **The Missing Link**, a macho amphibious throwback who talks like a retired action hero. The biggest and least verbal member of the group is **Insectosaurus**, a towering grub-like creature whose chief job is to make noise, look adorable in a catastrophic way, and remind viewers that DreamWorks knows how to sell plush toys.

The plot lurches into motion when an alien overlord named **Gallaxhar**, voiced by **Rainn Wilson**, sends a gigantic robot probe to Earth in search of the quantonium now inside Susan. With the military outmatched, the blustering General W.R. Monger — voiced by **Kiefer Sutherland** with cigar-chomping gusto — convinces the President, played broadly by **Stephen Colbert**, to release the monsters and use them as a last line of defense. The President’s attempt to communicate with the alien robot via a synthesizer performance is one of the movie’s sillier and more inspired jokes, a reminder that the film works best when it stops rushing and lets its absurdity breathe.

“Monsters vs. Aliens” is openly built from old science-fiction and horror matinee parts. Susan/Ginormica is an obvious riff on **“Attack of the 50 Foot Woman.”** B.O.B. channels the gelatinous menace of **“The Blob,”** though transformed into a friendly idiot. Dr. Cockroach evokes **“The Fly”** and the tradition of the doomed scientist undone by his own experiment. The Missing Link nods to **“Creature from the Black Lagoon,”** while Insectosaurus suggests the giant-bug panic of 1950s atomic-age cinema, from **“Them!”** to countless rubber-suited knockoffs. Even the robot attack carries echoes of Cold War alien-invasion classics, with a little **“War of the Worlds”** panic and **“The Day the Earth Stood Still”** imagery thrown in for good measure.

These references give the film a clever visual foundation, but they also reveal its limitation. “Monsters vs. Aliens” often seems more enthusiastic about recognizing old movies than reinventing them. The creature designs are appealing, and the action sequences are polished, particularly a large-scale battle on the Golden Gate Bridge. Yet much of the humor lands in the predictable DreamWorks zone: pop-culture winks, sarcastic asides, broad slapstick and jokes that feel engineered to keep adults mildly occupied while children enjoy the colors and collisions.

Still, there is a modestly effective emotional arc beneath the noise. Susan begins the film defined by her fiancé’s ambitions and her own desire for an ordinary life. Once transformed into Ginormica, she gradually discovers that being “normal” may have been an overrated goal, especially when the normal people around her prove shallow, cowardly or absurdly bureaucratic. Witherspoon gives Susan enough sincerity to keep this empowerment story from feeling entirely mechanical, though the screenplay announces its lessons with the subtlety of a falling meteor.

The supporting voice cast helps considerably. Rogen’s B.O.B. is the obvious scene-stealer, turning stupidity into a kind of blissful performance art. Laurie gives Dr. Cockroach a refined lunacy, and Arnett’s gravelly bravado makes The Missing Link funnier than his dialogue often deserves. Colbert’s President is amusing in short bursts, though the caricature wears thin. Wilson’s Gallaxhar, meanwhile, is more serviceable than memorable — a villain with a grand plan, a giant spaceship and not much personality beyond inflated self-regard.

Visually, the movie is slick and energetic, with the rounded, high-gloss finish typical of late-2000s studio animation. The 3-D presentation was clearly a major selling point at the time, and the film dutifully includes objects flying, falling and lunging toward the audience. Whether that amounts to cinematic immersion or merely a premium-ticket gimmick depends on one’s patience for spectacle as a substitute for surprise.

For younger viewers, “Monsters vs. Aliens” should provide enough momentum, creature comedy and action to satisfy. For adults, it is pleasant but thin — a film with a terrific premise, a strong voice cast and a shelf full of sci-fi references, but not quite enough wit or narrative daring to become the modern monster mash it wants to be. It is not a disaster from another planet. It is more like a well-built spacecraft that never reaches escape velocity.

**Rating: 2.5 out of 4 stars**  
**“Monsters vs. Aliens” is rated PG for sci-fi action, some crude humor and mild language. Running time: approximately 94 minutes.**

I can’t write it *as* a CNN review, but here’s an original 2009-style entertainment review in a mainstream news-magazine tone:

---

## Big Monsters, Bigger Effects, Small Story

**“Monsters vs. Aliens” arrives with a title that practically writes the pitch meeting for itself.** DreamWorks Animation has assembled a giant woman, a gelatinous blob, a mad scientist cockroach, a prehistoric fish-ape and an extraterrestrial invasion, then launched them at audiences in bright, expensive-looking 3-D. Add a roster of recognizable celebrity voices and a heroine-centered empowerment arc, and the result sounds, on paper, like an animated blockbuster with both spectacle and attitude.

The problem is that the movie rarely develops much beyond the pitch.

The story follows Susan Murphy, voiced by Reese Witherspoon, an ordinary bride-to-be who is struck by a meteor on her wedding day and grows to nearly 50 feet tall. Renamed “Ginormica” by the government, she is whisked away to a secret facility where other strange creatures have been hidden for decades. When an alien villain threatens Earth, Susan and her fellow monsters are recruited as humanity’s last line of defense.

It is a premise with plenty of comic potential, and at times the film takes advantage of it. The monster team — including Seth Rogen’s cheerful blob B.O.B., Hugh Laurie’s Dr. Cockroach, Will Arnett’s Missing Link and Kiefer Sutherland’s blustering military man — gives the movie a lively, joke-driven energy. Rogen in particular gets some of the biggest laughs, mostly by turning B.O.B.’s complete lack of intelligence into a reliable gag machine.

But “Monsters vs. Aliens” too often feels like a collection of concepts in search of a story. The movie has scale, color and noise, yet it lacks the emotional precision and narrative momentum that make the best animated films resonate beyond their novelty. The characters are introduced with flair, but most are reduced to one-note comic functions. The alien invasion is enormous, but oddly weightless. Even the villain, Gallaxhar, voiced by Rainn Wilson, is more a delivery system for jokes than a memorable threat.

The film’s most interesting idea is Susan’s transformation from sidelined fiancée to self-possessed hero. There is a clear attempt to give young viewers — especially girls — a message about confidence, independence and refusing to shrink oneself for someone else’s comfort. That angle gives the movie a welcome contemporary edge, and Witherspoon brings warmth and determination to the role.

Still, the empowerment theme is stronger in theory than in execution. Susan’s personal journey is easy to understand, but the screenplay rushes through it with broad strokes. Her fiancé, Derek, is written so obviously as a vain and self-absorbed obstacle that her eventual liberation from him carries less dramatic force than it should. The movie tells us Susan is discovering her strength, but it rarely slows down long enough to make that discovery feel surprising or deeply earned.

Visually, “Monsters vs. Aliens” is far more confident. Released in 3-D, the film clearly embraces the format, with objects flying toward the audience, large-scale action sequences and gleaming sci-fi environments designed to show off the technology. The animation is polished, and the creature designs have an appealing retro monster-movie charm. The film borrows affectionately from 1950s science fiction and creature features, though many of those references will likely register more with parents than with children.

That split is part of the movie’s larger issue. It wants to be a parody, an action spectacle, a family comedy and a girl-power adventure all at once. None of those ambitions is misguided, but the film never blends them into something fully satisfying. The jokes come quickly, but not all land. The action is busy, but not especially suspenseful. The emotional beats are clear, but thin.

Compared with DreamWorks’ strongest animated efforts, “Monsters vs. Aliens” feels engineered more than inspired. It has the ingredients of a hit: a marketable title, a high-concept premise, a starry cast, eye-catching 3-D and enough pop-culture humor to keep adults awake. What it does not have is a story sturdy enough to support all that machinery.

Children may enjoy the slapstick, the bright visuals and the sheer absurdity of a giant woman fighting aliens with a blob and a cockroach scientist. Adults may appreciate some of the genre references and the film’s brisk pace. But once the 3-D glasses come off, there is not much left to think about.

For a movie about gigantic creatures and intergalactic warfare, “Monsters vs. Aliens” feels surprisingly small.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a sarcastic entertainment review of “Monsters vs. Aliens” that opens with an alarmist joke, summarizes Susan/Ginormica’s origin and monster teammates, lists classic sci-fi inspirations, and concludes that the movie is mediocre but harmless.
counterfactuals.output:
**Warning: giant women, gelatinous blobs, and government cover-ups have invaded family entertainment—please remain calm and purchase popcorn.**

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is DreamWorks’ 2009 animated attempt to ask the timeless question: what if classic B-movie creatures had self-esteem issues and were voiced by famous people? The result is a bright, busy, mildly amusing sci-fi spoof that never quite becomes monstrous enough to be memorable or alien enough to feel fresh.

The story begins with Susan Murphy, a perfectly normal bride-to-be whose wedding day is rudely interrupted by a meteor full of “quantonium.” Instead of receiving a toaster or a meaningful partnership, Susan becomes 49 feet 11 inches tall and is promptly renamed **Ginormica** by the government, because apparently the secret military’s branding department is run by a middle-schooler. She is whisked away to a hidden facility where America stores its inconvenient monsters, which feels about right.

Her new teammates include **B.O.B.**, a blue gelatinous blob with no brain but plenty of confidence; **Dr. Cockroach**, a mad scientist who turned himself into, yes, a cockroach; **The Missing Link**, a fish-ape hybrid with faded macho swagger; and **Insectosaurus**, a gigantic bug who mostly communicates by screaming and being large. Together, they are recruited to fight an alien invasion led by the evil Gallaxhar, who wants the quantonium for the usual villain reasons: power, domination, and a firm commitment to theatrical self-importance.

The film cheerfully raids the attic of classic science fiction and monster cinema. Susan/Ginormica is an obvious nod to **Attack of the 50 Foot Woman**. B.O.B. recalls **The Blob**. Dr. Cockroach channels **The Fly** and old mad-scientist creature features. The Missing Link winks at **Creature from the Black Lagoon**, while Insectosaurus evokes giant-bug movies like **Mothra** and **Them!** Gallaxhar and the alien-robot spectacle pull from 1950s flying-saucer paranoia, **War of the Worlds**, and the general Cold War-era tradition of pointing at the sky and panicking.

As entertainment, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is perfectly adequate, which is both its charm and its curse. The animation is colorful, the voice cast works hard, and a few jokes land with respectable force. But the movie often feels like it is checking boxes rather than unleashing chaos: empowering heroine, wacky sidekicks, pop-culture spoofing, big climax, lesson learned, please exit through the gift shop.

Still, it is difficult to dislike too strongly. It is loud but not obnoxious, silly but not painful, and clever just often enough to avoid becoming a total government experiment gone wrong. In the end, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is mediocre but harmless—a perfectly serviceable animated diversion for anyone who has ever thought, “I’d like my creature-feature homage with more celebrity voices and fewer surprises.”
